title: The Snake's Pass
description: Published in 1890 and Stoker's first novel: a romance of the west of Ireland, of a lost treasure, a land dispute and a peasant legend of the Snake's Pass.
plot_or_argument: Arthur Severn comes to the Mayo coast, falls in love with Norah Joyce, and becomes involved in the struggle over the land and the buried gold of the hill; the villain Murdock is exposed and the legend of the snake is explained.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Irish Land War, the Congested Districts, and the folklore of the west of Ireland.
literary_significance: The Snake's Pass is a significant Irish regional novel of the Land War and the earliest evidence of Stoker's interest in folklore and in the power of place.

title: The Jewel of Seven Stars
description: Published in 1903 and the most Egyptological of Stoker's novels: the attempt to revive the mummy of the ancient Egyptian queen Tera, and the terror that follows the experiment.
plot_or_argument: Margaret Trelawny's father is found in a trance in his study surrounded by Egyptian antiquities; the investigation by Sergeant Daw and the scholar Corbeck reveals that Tera's mummy and jewels have been assembled in England, and the attempt to resurrect her ends in catastrophe.
historical_context: The 1890s-1900s, the Egyptian mummy-unwrapping craze, the archaeology of the Valley of the Kings, and the Victorian occult revival.
literary_significance: The Jewel of Seven Stars is the central English mummy novel and a key text of the literature of Egyptology and imperial archaeology.

title: Under the Sunset
description: Published in 1881 and Stoker's first book: eight fairy tales set in a land beyond the sunset, written for children and darker than the Victorian norm.
plot_or_argument: The tales include 'Under the Sunset', in which two children visit the country of the dead, 'The Rose Prince', 'The Invisible Giant', and 'The Shadow Builder', in which a boy's shadow becomes a tyrant.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Victorian fairy-tale revival and the death of Stoker's infant son.
literary_significance: Under the Sunset is an important late-Victorian children's collection and the earliest statement of Stoker's preoccupation with death, shadows and the border between worlds.

title: A Study in Scarlet
description: Published in Beeton's Christmas Annual in 1887 and the first appearance of Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson: the investigation of a corpse in an empty Brixton house, and the revenge that reaches back to the Mormon migration.
plot_or_argument: Watson, returned from Afghanistan, lodges with Holmes in Baker Street and accompanies him to the scene of a murder; Holmes deduces the killer from the cab, the ring and the word 'Rache', traces the crime to Jefferson Hope, and explains the Mormon persecution of the Drebber and Stangerson families in Utah.
principal_characters: Sherlock Holmes; Doctor John Watson; Inspector Lestrade; Jefferson Hope; Enoch Drebber; Joseph Stangerson; Tobias Gregson
historical_context: The 1880s, the new detective police at Scotland Yard, the Afghan war, and the Mormon emigration to Utah.
literary_significance: A Study in Scarlet founded the modern detective novel in English: the partnership of the consulting detective and the medical narrator, the Baker Street rooms and the chain of deduction became the permanent furniture of the genre.

title: The Sign of Four
description: Published in Lippincott's in 1890 in the same issue as the first version of Dorian Gray: a case that begins with a missing officer, a pearl and a cipher, and ends with the Agra treasure and the Andaman Islander Tonga.
plot_or_argument: Mary Morstan receives pearls from an unknown benefactor and consults Holmes; the investigation leads to the death of Bartholomew Sholto, the one-legged Jonathan Small and his companion Tonga, and the treasure lost in the Thames. Watson marries Mary Morstan.
principal_characters: Sherlock Holmes; Doctor John Watson; Mary Morstan; Thaddeus Sholto; Jonathan Small; Tonga; Athelney Jones; Major Sholto
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, the Indian Mutiny of 1857, the Andaman Islands penal colony, and the opium dens of London.
literary_significance: The Sign of Four is the fullest of the early Holmes novels and the most explicitly imperial: its plot turns on the loot of the Mutiny and on the colonial servant's revenge, and its atmosphere of fog, river and labyrinth set the tone of the London detective story.

title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
description: Published in 1892, collecting the twelve stories that appeared in the Strand Magazine from July 1891: the volume that created the modern short detective story and made Holmes a national institution.
plot_or_argument: The twelve cases include 'A Scandal in Bohemia', in which Irene Adler outwits Holmes; 'The Red-Headed League', a bank robbery disguised as a sinecure; 'The Speckled Band', a murder by snake; 'The Blue Carbuncle', a Christmas goose; and 'The Final Problem', in which Holmes and Moriarty fall at the Reichenbach Falls.
principal_characters: Sherlock Holmes; Doctor John Watson; Mrs Hudson; Inspector Lestrade; Irene Adler; Professor Moriarty; the King of Bohemia; Helen Stoner
literary_form: Collection of twelve short stories (Strand Magazine, 1891-92)
historical_context: The 1890s, the new mass-circulation illustrated magazine, the suburban railway and the telegraph, and the professionalisation of the detective.
literary_significance: The Adventures created the modern short story of detection and the serial character who outlives his author; its formula — a problem, a client, a chain of inference and a final explanation — became the template for the entire genre.

title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
description: Serialised in the Strand from August 1901 and published in 1902, set before the Reichenbach Falls: the most famous of all detective novels, and the one that fuses the ratiocinative plot with the Gothic horror of the moor.
plot_or_argument: Sir Charles Baskerville dies of fright on the moor, and Holmes sends Watson to Devon with Sir Henry Baskerville; the hound is a painted and phosphorescent animal kept by the naturalist Stapleton, a Baskerville descendant, who hopes to inherit the estate. Holmes arrives, the hound is shot, and Stapleton is lost in the Grimpen Mire.
principal_characters: Sherlock Holmes; Doctor John Watson; Sir Henry Baskerville; Stapleton; Beryl Stapleton; Dr Mortimer; Laura Lyons; Selden; Sir Charles Baskerville
historical_context: The 1880s-90s, Dartmoor and its legends, the Victorian folklore of the spectral hound, and the naturalist's collecting culture.
literary_significance: The Hound of the Baskervilles is the most widely read detective novel in English and the great English example of the Gothic detective story; its moor, its hound and its rational explanation of a supernatural legend are the classic statement of the genre's double logic.

title: The White Company
description: Published in 1891 and Doyle's own favourite among his books: a romance of the Hundred Years' War, following the young archer Alleyne Edricson to the wars in France with the free company of Sir Nigel Loring.
plot_or_argument: Alleyne leaves the abbey of Beaulieu, joins the White Company under Sir Nigel Loring, campaigns in Spain and France, rescues the Lady Maude and is knighted after the battle of Najera.
historical_context: The 1360s-70s, the free companies of the Hundred Years' War, the English longbow, and the Victorian chivalric revival.
literary_significance: The White Company is the finest English historical romance of the fourteenth century and the central text of the Victorian revival of medieval chivalry; it made Doyle as a historical novelist as well as a detective writer.

title: The Lost World
description: Published in the Strand in 1912 and the founding text of the dinosaur adventure: Professor Challenger's expedition to a South American plateau where the prehistoric world survives.
plot_or_argument: The journalist Edward Malone joins Challenger, Professor Summerlee and Lord John Roxton on an expedition to the Amazonian plateau; they find dinosaurs, ape-men and a lost tribe, escape with a pterodactyl, and Challenger exhibits it at the Zoological Institute.
principal_characters: Professor George Edward Challenger; Edward Malone; Professor Summerlee; Lord John Roxton; Zambo; Gladys Hungerton
historical_context: The 1910s, the age of polar and Amazonian exploration, and the new palaeontology of the dinosaur.
literary_significance: The Lost World founded the lost-world romance and gave the twentieth century its most durable adventure formula; its mixture of scientific speculation and imperial exploration is a key text in the literature of the popular scientific romance.

title: The Time Machine
description: Published in 1895 and the founding work of the modern scientific romance: the journey of an inventor to the year 802,701, where he finds the Eloi and the Morlocks, and to the last days of the earth.
plot_or_argument: The Time Traveller demonstrates his machine, travels to the far future, discovers a pastoral people served by a subterranean race, loses his machine to the Morlocks, escapes to the year thirty million, and returns to tell the tale before vanishing on a second journey.
narrative_structure: Framed narrative: the Time Traveller's account to a dinner party, with an epilogue by the narrator.
principal_characters: The Time Traveller; the Eloi; the Morlocks; Weena; the Medical Man; the Psychologist; the Editor
historical_context: The 1890s, the second law of thermodynamics and the 'heat death' of the universe, the Darwinian and socialist thought of the period, and the class divisions of Victorian London.
literary_significance: The Time Machine invented the time-travel story and gave the scientific romance its method: the extrapolation of a social and biological idea into a narrative. Its vision of class division becoming speciation is the most powerful single image in Victorian science fiction.

title: The War of the Worlds
description: Published in 1898 and the most famous of all invasion narratives: the Martian landing in Surrey, the destruction of the Home Counties, and the defeat of the invaders by the bacteria of earth.
plot_or_argument: Cylinders fall on Horsell Common and the Martians emerge with heat-rays and tripods; the narrator flees through London and Surrey, witnesses the rout of the army, is trapped with the curate, and emerges to find the Martians dead of a bacterial infection.
principal_characters: The narrator; the curate; the artilleryman; the Martian fighting-machines; Ogilvy the astronomer; Henderson
historical_context: The 1890s, the imperial rivalry of the European powers, the British conquest of Tasmania as a model for extermination, and the new bacteriology of Koch and Pasteur.
literary_significance: The War of the Worlds is the founding text of the alien-invasion narrative and the great English fable of reverse colonisation; its Darwinian ending is a permanent rebuke to the imperial assumption of moral superiority.

title: The Invisible Man: A Grotesque Romance
description: Published in 1897: the story of Griffin, a scientist who makes himself invisible and is destroyed by the consequences of his own discovery.
plot_or_argument: Griffin takes refuge in the village of Iping, robs and terrorises the neighbourhood, takes shelter with Dr Kemp and reveals his plan for a reign of terror, and is hunted and killed by the mob in Port Burdock.
principal_characters: Griffin; Doctor Kemp; Mrs Hall; Mr Marvel; Doctor Cuss; Colonel Adye
historical_context: The 1890s, the physics of light and refraction, the new research university, and the English fear of the unregulated scientist.
literary_significance: The Invisible Man is the classic English fable of the scientist without a moral community: its subject is not invisibility but the isolation and violence it produces, and it founded the modern literature of the dangerous discovery.

title: The Island of Doctor Moreau
description: Published in 1896 and the most disturbing of Wells's early romances: the story of a shipwrecked man who finds on a Pacific island a physiologist who turns animals into human beings.
plot_or_argument: Edward Prendick is rescued by the schooner Ipecacuanha, is put ashore on Moreau's island, and discovers that the vivisectionist is creating the Beast Folk, who live under a Law spoken by Moreau and his assistant Montgomery; Moreau is killed by a puma-woman, Montgomery dies, and Prendick returns to England to a horror of his own species.
principal_characters: Edward Prendick; Doctor Moreau; Montgomery; the Beast Folk; M'ling; the Sayer of the Law
historical_context: The 1890s, the anti-vivisection movement, the Darwinian account of the continuity of species, and the imperial logic of the colonial laboratory.
literary_significance: The Island of Doctor Moreau is the central English text on vivisection, evolution and the fear of the animal within; its images of the Law, the Beast Folk and the return to the beast made it a permanent point of reference for posthumanist criticism.

title: The Wheels of Chance: A Bicycling Idyll
description: Published in 1896 and the most charming of the early Wells novels: the story of a draper's assistant on a bicycling holiday who rescues a young woman from a predatory novelist, and learns that romance belongs to a class he cannot enter.
plot_or_argument: Hooper, a draper's assistant, sets off on a bicycle tour of the south of England, meets Jessie Milton, rescues her from the pursuit of Bechamel, rides with her to the coast, and returns to his shop after a brief and poignant adventure.
historical_context: The 1890s, the bicycle craze, the new leisure of the working man, the drapery trade, and the beginnings of the 'New Woman' on wheels.
literary_significance: The Wheels of Chance is the finest English novel of the bicycle and one of the first to record the democratisation of travel by the new machine; its class comedy makes it a key text of the 1890s.

title: Kipps: The Story of a Simple Soul
description: Published in 1905 and the first of Wells's great comic novels of class: the story of Arthur Kipps, draper's assistant, who inherits a fortune and discovers that money cannot buy the manners, taste or confidence of the English middle class.
plot_or_argument: Kipps inherits a legacy and is propelled into the genteel leisure class he cannot inhabit; he is humiliated at a literary society, lost among builders and servants, and finally rescued by his marriage to his childhood sweetheart Ann, and the novel ends with the small happiness of a man who has stopped trying to be something else.
historical_context: The 1900s, the English class system in the decade of the great estates and the new professional classes, and Wells's own youthful apprenticeship in drapery.
literary_significance: Kipps is the finest English novel of the modest man made rich and the funniest of Wells's books; its treatment of class as a matter of accent, taste and competence is a permanent contribution to the sociology of English manners.

title: Nature (1836)
description: Published anonymously in 1836 and the founding document of American Transcendentalism: a short book arguing that nature is the visible manifestation of spirit and that the individual may know God directly through it.
plot_or_argument: Emerson divides the essay into Nature, Commodity, Beauty, Language, Discipline, Idealism, Spirit and Prospects, and argues in each that the natural world is a symbol of the mind's own laws and that 'the kingdom of man over nature' is available to anyone who will look with fresh eyes.
historical_context: The 1830s, the American Unitarian crisis, the German idealism of Kant and Coleridge, and the new science of natural history.
literary_significance: Nature is the founding text of American Transcendentalism and of the American literature of nature: its call to look at the world with new eyes set the agenda for Thoreau, Whitman and the whole tradition of American nature writing.

title: 'The American Scholar'
description: Delivered at Harvard on 31 August 1837 and published the same year: the address Oliver Wendell Holmes called 'our intellectual Declaration of Independence'.
plot_or_argument: Emerson argues that the American scholar must draw his education from nature, from books and from action, and that the true scholar is 'Man Thinking'; he attacks the bookworm, the parrot of other men's thinking, and calls for an original American literature.
historical_context: The 1837, the American literary nationalism of the 1830s, the Harvard Phi Beta Kappa society, and the Panic of 1837.
literary_significance: 'The American Scholar' is the founding manifesto of American literary independence and one of the most influential addresses in American cultural history: it defined the intellectual vocation for the American writer and made originality a national duty.

title: Divinity School Address
description: Delivered on 15 July 1838 and the most controversial religious address in American history: an attack on the historical Christianity of the churches in the name of the soul's immediate access to God.
plot_or_argument: Emerson tells the graduating ministers that the church has made Jesus a historical idol, that the miracles and the scriptures have replaced the inward revelation, and that the preacher must speak from his own experience of the divine or not at all.
historical_context: The 1838, the Unitarian controversy, the Transcendentalist revolt against Boston Unitarianism, and the American revival of the 1830s.
literary_significance: The Divinity School Address is the founding text of American religious liberalism: it scandalised the Unitarian establishment, cost Emerson his Harvard invitations for thirty years, and gave American Transcendentalism its theology of the soul.

title: 'Self-Reliance'
description: Published in Essays: First Series in 1841 and the most influential essay in American literature: the argument that the individual must trust his own thought against the whole weight of society, custom and history.
plot_or_argument: Emerson denounces conformity, consistency, philanthropy and travel as escapes from the self, and insists that 'whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist'; the essay builds an ethic of self-trust from the doctrine that the soul in each person is the same universal soul.
historical_context: The 1840, the American democratic experiment, the reform movements of the 1840s, and the Romantic philosophy of the self.
literary_significance: 'Self-Reliance' is the central statement of American individualism and one of the most quoted essays in the language: it has shaped American ideas of the self, of originality and of dissent from Emerson's own day to the present.

title: Representative Men
description: Published in 1850 and the fullest statement of Emerson's theory of great men: studies of Plato, Swedenborg, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Napoleon and Goethe.
plot_or_argument: Emerson argues that each great man is a 'representative' of a faculty or an idea — the philosopher, the mystic, the sceptic, the poet, the man of the world, the writer — and that the study of great persons is the study of what the age needed and produced.
historical_context: The 1840s, the American lecture circuit, the Carlylean cult of the hero, and the democratic objection to hero-worship.
literary_significance: Representative Men is the central American statement of the philosophy of great men and a key text in the American reception of European culture; its essays on Montaigne and Shakespeare are among the best short criticism of the century.

title: English Traits
description: Published in 1856 and the most acute American book on England: a series of chapters on the English race, land, aristocracy, universities, religion, literature and character, drawn from three visits.
plot_or_argument: Emerson describes the English as a nation of shopkeepers with an instinct for the sea, a genius for the practical, and a brutal class system; his portraits of the aristocracy, the Toryism of the English mind and the English Sunday are comic, exact and unsentimental.
historical_context: The 1850s, the Anglo-American literary relations of the period, the Great Exhibition of 1851, and the American debate on English institutions.
literary_significance: English Traits is the best portrait of the English national character by an American and a key text in the literature of national character; it shaped the American image of England for a generation.

title: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
description: Published in 1854 after nine years of revision and the central text of American nature writing: the account of two years, two months and two days in a cabin at Walden Pond, and of an experiment in living deliberately.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau describes the building of the house, the economy of his life, the reading of the classics, the sounds and visitors of the woods, the bean field, the pond, the animals, the seasons and the spring thaw, and ends with the parable of the artist of Kouroo.
historical_context: The 1845-47, Concord and the Transcendentalist circle, the Mexican War and the market revolution, and the American debate on labour and simplicity.
literary_significance: Walden is the founding text of American nature writing and one of the great works of American prose: it is at once a manual of economy, a naturalist's journal, a spiritual autobiography and a political argument, and it has shaped the modern environmental movement more than any other book.

title: 'Resistance to Civil Government' ('Civil Disobedience')
description: Published in Aesthetic Papers in 1849 after Thoreau's night in the Concord jail in 1846: the founding modern argument for the primacy of individual conscience over the state.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau argues that a government that permits slavery and wages an unjust war forfeits the citizen's obedience; he describes his refusal to pay the poll tax, his imprisonment, and the principle that the individual must withdraw cooperation from injustice even at the cost of punishment.
historical_context: The 1846-49, the Mexican War, the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850 to come, the abolitionist movement, and the Concord jail.
literary_significance: 'Civil Disobedience' is the founding text of the modern theory of non-violent resistance: it shaped Tolstoy, Gandhi, Martin Luther King and the whole tradition of conscientious objection, and it is one of the most influential essays in the language.

title: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
description: Published in 1849 and written as an elegy for Thoreau's brother John, who died in 1842: an account of a river journey in a rowing boat, with digressions on friendship, poetry, history and religion.
plot_or_argument: The brothers row from Concord up the Merrimack over a week in 1839; the narrative of the river is interrupted by essays on the Indian languages, on Chaucer and Ossian, on friendship and on the death of a brother.
historical_context: The 1839 journey, the American enthusiasm for the picturesque river voyage, and the Transcendentalist interest in Eastern scripture.
literary_significance: A Week is Thoreau's first book and the finest American example of the travel narrative as meditation: its elegy for his brother is one of the most moving passages in American prose, and its hybrid of journey and essay invented a form that American writing still uses.

title: 'Slavery in Massachusetts'
description: Delivered at Framingham on 4 July 1854 and published in the Liberator: Thoreau's furious response to the rendition of the fugitive slave Anthony Burns from Boston.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau attacks the state of Massachusetts for returning Burns, charges the press and the churches with complicity, and declares that the abolitionist must act against the government rather than petition it.
historical_context: The 1854, the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and the abolitionist movement in Boston.
literary_significance: 'Slavery in Massachusetts' is the most radical of Thoreau's political essays and a founding document of American abolitionist literature: it marks the moment when the Transcendentalists turned from moral suasion to political resistance.
